source.title: Beyond Sunk Costs: Boosting LLM Pre-training Efficiency via Orthogonal Growth of Mixture-of-Experts
source.authors: Ruizhe Wang; Yu-Cheng Ding; Xiao Liu; Yao-Xiang Wang; Peng Cheng; Bai-Ning Guo; Zhengjun Zha; Yeyun Gong

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares architecture variants at similar parameter counts and reports training-loss outcomes, conceptually testing V4. It does not fit or test the scaling laws themselves.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. and uses the Chinchilla compute estimate to define a convergence threshold; it does not test that estimate or fit power laws. Its weight-norm patterns, growth-efficiency results, and downstream-accuracy results do not establish the predictability named in the other versions.
record.test_reason: This is a model-growth methods paper. It uses the Chinchilla D=20N ratio and 6ND as a reference point (Fc) for growth timing, and reports how well its own growth methods perform. It fits no power laws, and none of its comparisons hold parameter count fixed while varying shape. Interposition and stacking yield the same architecture (same depth, width and experts) and differ only in how the copied layers are ordered at initialization. So the stack-vs-interposition loss gap is an initialization or growth-strategy effect, not a test of V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is incomplete. The authors conclude that converged MoE checkpoints can be recycled by orthogonal growth: interpositional depth growth plus noisy expert duplication. They find interposition beats stacking beyond about 1× Chinchilla-optimal FLOPs. Final performance correlates positively with sunk cost. Growth matches or beats scratch training at fixed total FLOPs. At 17B→70B over 1T tokens, the grown model gains 10.6% relative accuracy over scratch at the same extra compute. They draw no conclusions about scaling-law fits.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates model-growth strategies and training outcomes rather than fitting loss-scaling laws or testing their extrapolations. It uses a cited compute-optimal estimate as a reference point.
record.method_sensitivity: The comparison between layer-growth methods depends on growth timing: the authors place the onset of interposition's advantage at approximately 1× Fc. They also report that its advantage persists at growth factor k=4.

fits_no_version.finding: For grown 6B MoE models given a fixed extra budget of 3e20 FLOPs, final accuracy rises with the sunk FLOPs of the base checkpoint. End accuracy goes from 38.79 (from scratch) to about 48.99 (88k-step base) (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Performance after model growth increases with the pre-growth compute invested in the base checkpoint.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed total FLOPs budget, grown models match or slightly exceed a 6B model trained from scratch. Example end accuracies: 47.66–48.53 vs 45.03 (Table 5). Growth underperforms when started from very late checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Growing a smaller pretrained model is compute-equivalent or better than scratch training at equal total compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Interposition beats stacking only once base training exceeds about 1× Chinchilla-optimal FLOPs (Fc). Stacking is comparable or better below that point (Figure 4; Tables 12–19).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The best layer-growth strategy depends on how far the base model has trained relative to compute-optimal.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: For the relevant loss comparisons, the figures provide no extracted numerical values or uncertainty estimates; the text states directions of effects but not their magnitude. The architecture comparison covers selected MoE growth settings rather than a broad architecture sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were retained. Other reported results concern weight norms, growth efficiency, and downstream accuracy, rather than measures named by the tested claim version; cited scaling-law results are not the study's own results.

untested.parts: Uses the Chinchilla D=20N ratio as a reference but does not test allocation across budgets.
No fixed-parameter shape sweep. Depth-grown and width-grown 6B models differ in active parameters (1.0B vs 892M) and are confounded by growth initialization.
No other modalities, repeated data, or transfer scaling.
Reports downstream accuracy over training but does not relate it to scale or to loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V4, but stack and interposition growth yield identical architectures, so there is no shape variation at fixed parameter count. All rows also compare the study's own method with a baseline. Chinchilla is used only as a tool to define Fc, so the study is classed T4, uses_without_test. The abstract's mention of 'scaling laws analysis' refers to the sunk-cost correlation, not to power-law fits.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on smaller runs predict much larger runs.
The paper uses a cited compute-optimal ratio to estimate a threshold but does not optimize parameter/token allocations across compute budgets.
Only selected MoE layer-growth variants are compared; the study does not survey a wide range of architectures or isolate depth, width, and other architecture variables comprehensively.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The paper reports downstream evaluations but does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.

reader_labels.reason: The reported loss comparison favors interposition over stacking in several settings, but the paper does not quantify whether the differences are slight and tests only selected growth variants; see r1–r7.
